items.title: Harbour Sports Club membership
items.context: A man phones a sports club to join.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good morning, Harbour Sports Club, Emma speaking. How can I help?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Hi there. I'd like to become a member, please. I've just moved to the area.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lovely. I can take your details over the phone and get the form started for you. Could I have your name first?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Yes, it's Jonathan Fairfax.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Could you spell your surname for me?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Of course. It's F-A-I-R-F-A-X.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Fairfax, thank you. And what's your address?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: It's 72 Weston Road. Oh, sorry, no, that was my old flat. It's number 27 Weston Road.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 27 Weston Road. And the postcode?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: It's BH6 4TR. That's B-H-6, then 4-T-R.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Great. What's the best phone number to reach you on?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: There's a landline at the house, but I'm hardly ever in. My mobile is best. It's 07734 519208.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 07734 519208. Thanks. Now, we like to know which activities members are most interested in, so we can send the right timetables.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Well, I was thinking about tennis, but I hear the courts are booked up most evenings. So I'd say swimming, mainly in the evenings after work.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Evening swimming. The pool's open until ten, so that should suit you.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Perfect.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And which type of membership would you like? We have individual, couple and family.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: I was going to go for individual, but my wife and our two kids want to come along too, so I think family makes more sense.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: No problem. And would you prefer to pay annually or monthly?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Monthly, please. How much would that be?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: The individual rate is 38 pounds a month, but the family membership is 45 pounds a month, and that covers two adults and up to three children.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: That's very reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Can I ask how you heard about us? Was it through our website?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: No, actually. A neighbour mentioned you, but what made me call was a poster I saw in the library.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Oh good, so they did put it up. Now, when would you like your membership to start?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Could I start on Monday?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: I'm afraid the pool is closed on Mondays this month for maintenance. How about Tuesday?

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: Tuesday's fine.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And one last thing. When you come in, please don't use the south car park, because it's being resurfaced. Use the north car park, which is right next to the main entrance.

transcript.speaker: Jonathan
transcript.text: The north car park. Got it. Thanks so much for your help.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: You're welcome, Mr Fairfax. We'll see you on Tuesday.

items.title: Ashford Maritime Museum
items.context: A guide welcomes a group of visitors to a maritime museum.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Ashford Maritime Museum. My name's Daniel, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Before you head off to explore, I'd like to give you a quick introduction to the building and tell you what you'll find in each area.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A lot of visitors assume this building was once a fish market, because the fish quay is just outside the front door.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: In fact, it was built in 1842 as the town's customs house, where merchants paid tax on the goods their ships brought in.
keywords: built in 1842 as the town's customs house

answerTags.after: built in 1842 as the town's customs house

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It only became a museum in the 1970s, after the shipbuilders' warehouse next door was knocked down.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Now, some news for regular visitors. Entry is still seven pounds for adults, I'm afraid, so it hasn't become free, although under-sixteens still get in without paying.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: What has changed is that since April we've extended our opening hours, so we now close at six rather than five.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: We're also hoping to launch an audio guide app, but that won't be ready until next year.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: So, where to start? Most people go straight into the Harbour Gallery, but I'd suggest you begin with the short film in the Orientation Room.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It's only twelve minutes long and it gives you a timeline that makes everything else much easier to follow.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A quick practical point: reception no longer has space to store luggage, so any large bags must go in the lockers on the lower ground floor.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Right, the areas themselves. The Harbour Gallery has our collection of oil paintings of the port.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Some of them are very fragile, so please keep your cameras and phones away in there. Photography isn't allowed in that gallery at all.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Next door is the Shipwreck Room. We used to run free guided talks in there, but these days it's self-guided.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The highlight is the original captain's log from the Mary Ellen, along with letters written by her crew, the real documents, not copies.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Then there's the Lighthouse Tower. You can climb all ninety steps, but it costs an extra two pounds on top of your ticket.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: People expect a spectacular view from the top, but to be honest the windows are rather small.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: On the first floor you'll find the Rope Workshop. At eleven and at two, one of our volunteers shows you how rope was made by hand, so you can watch the whole process live.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have children with you, head for the Children's Deck. They can dress up as sailors, try tying knots and steer a model ship, so it's all hands-on.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: I should mention that the Navigation Room on the same floor is temporarily closed while we repair the roof.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: And finally, the Captain's Café on the top floor. The cakes are excellent, but the real reason to go up is the terrace.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: From there you get the best view of the town and the whole harbour, much better than from the tower.
keywords: the best view of the town

answerTags.after: the best view of the town

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The café stays open until half past five, so there's plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: If you have any questions, you'll find me or one of the other guides in the entrance hall.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Enjoy your visit, everyone.

items.title: Choosing a research topic
items.context: A tutor and a student, Maya, discuss her research project.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Come in, Maya. Have a seat. How's the project planning going?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Better, I think. I've narrowed it down to two ideas since our last meeting.
keywords: narrowed it down to two ideas

answerTags.after: narrowed it down to two ideas

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. I know you were worried about the proposal deadline, but that's not for another fortnight, so there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: So, you mentioned last week you were thinking about urban noise.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I was, and there's actually plenty of research on it. But honestly the data collection would have taken the whole term. I'd need readings from dozens of sites.
keywords: data collection would have taken the whole term

answerTags.after: data collection would have taken the whole term

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That's a fair point. So what have you settled on instead?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I did consider air quality in city parks, but I'm leaning towards rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature.
keywords: rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature

answerTags.after: rooftop gardens and how they affect building temperature

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Interesting. There's quite a lot published on that already, isn't there?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: There is, which is actually why I like it. It won't save me any time reading, but I can compare my results with earlier studies.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Good. And where would you take your measurements? Not in the lab, I hope.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: No. The library has a green roof, and the facilities team said I could use it from next month.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Make sure you get that permission in writing. Facilities staff change, and you don't want to lose access halfway through.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: I'll email them today. What about equipment? I'd looked at buying temperature loggers online, but they're quite expensive.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Don't spend your own money on them.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: No, I'll borrow temperature loggers from the geography department instead. They have about twenty.
keywords: borrow temperature loggers from the geography department

answerTags.after: borrow temperature loggers from the geography department

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Twenty should be plenty. Now, the timetable. Your literature review was originally due in week four, but we've moved it. It needs to be finished by week six.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Week six. OK. Should I include studies from other countries?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Yes, and they don't all have to be recent ones. But focus on cities with a similar climate to ours, otherwise the comparison won't hold.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: That makes sense. I'd also thought about interviewing the building managers.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: That would be nice to have, but it's not essential. I'd leave it unless you have spare time.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Fair enough. And the final report, is it still four thousand words?

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Three and a half thousand, plus appendices. And keep the method section short. Examiners care much more about your analysis.

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Got it. Short method, more analysis.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Is there anything else you're unsure about?

transcript.speaker: Maya
transcript.text: Not right now. I'll send you a draft outline by Friday.

transcript.speaker: Tutor
transcript.text: Perfect. Good luck, Maya.

items.title: Urban heat islands
items.context: A lecturer explains why cities are warmer than the countryside and what can be done about it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today we're looking at a phenomenon that affects almost every large city on the planet: the urban heat island.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Put simply, an urban heat island is a built-up area that is noticeably warmer than the countryside around it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The effect was first described in the early nineteenth century by Luke Howard, an amateur scientist who is better known for naming the clouds.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Howard kept careful temperature records in London and compared them with readings taken in nearby villages.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So how big is the difference? You will sometimes read that city centres can be twelve degrees warmer, but that figure comes from a single, very unusual night.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: A more typical maximum is around seven degrees, and in most cities the average difference is much smaller.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Interestingly, the gap is not greatest in the middle of a hot afternoon, as you might expect.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It is actually at night that the difference is most marked, because the city releases the heat it has stored during the day.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: That brings us to the causes. The first is the materials we build with.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Dark surfaces, and asphalt in particular, absorb a great deal of solar energy and then give it off slowly for hours.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Concrete and brick behave in a similar way, though they are generally a little paler.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The second cause is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants and moist soil cool the air through evaporation.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In a city, rainwater is quickly carried away by drains, so there is far less moisture available for this natural cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The third cause is waste heat. Vehicles contribute, of course, but a surprisingly large share is released by buildings, through heating systems, lighting and machinery.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: And the shape of the city matters too: tall buildings along narrow streets trap warm air and block the wind.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Why does any of this matter? Hotter cities use more energy for cooling, and air pollution tends to be worse.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: But the most serious concern is health. During heatwaves, the group most at risk is the elderly, particularly those who live alone.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Young children are also vulnerable, but studies consistently show the highest death rates among older people.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what can planners do? One simple approach is so-called cool roofs.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: These are roofs painted white or covered with light materials so that they reflect sunlight rather than absorbing it.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Another is to increase green space. Many people assume that grass is enough, but in fact it provides relatively little cooling.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The most effective measure is planting trees along streets, because they provide shade as well as releasing moisture.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, cities need better data. Here in our own city, researchers originally planned to use weather balloons.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Instead, they attached two hundred small sensors to lampposts, which now record temperature every ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The results have already shown which neighbourhoods need the most urgent attention.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In next week's session we'll look at some of that data in detail, so please read chapter five before then.

items.title: Westbridge Language Centre enrolment
items.context: A man phones a language centre to enrol on an evening course.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good morning, Westbridge Language Centre. How can I help you?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Hi. I'd like to enrol on one of your evening courses, please.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Of course. I'll fill in the form for you now. Could I have your surname first?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, it's Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Thank you. And your first name?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Daniel.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: And which language are you interested in, Daniel?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Well, at first I was thinking about Italian, because I'm visiting Rome next year. But actually I use Spanish much more for work, so Spanish, please.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Fine. Have you studied it before?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Yes, I did two years at school, so I'm not really a beginner. I took your online test last week and it put me at intermediate level.
keywords: it put me at intermediate level

answerTags.after: it put me at intermediate level

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Great, intermediate it is. Now, can I take your address?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: It's 42 Harcourt Road, that's H-A-R-C-O-U-R-T, here in Westbridge.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Lovely. And a contact number?

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: My mobile is 07845 219630.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: 07845 219630. Now, the intermediate Spanish group meets on two evenings. The Tuesday class is already full, I'm afraid, but there are still a few places on Thursday.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Thursday is fine for me. I finish work early that day anyway.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Good. Let me tell you a few practical things. The classes used to be in the main hall, but that's being renovated this term, so they'll be held in the library building instead, on the second floor.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: The library building. OK, I know where that is.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: As for the fee, the standard price for the ten-week course is £210.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Oh, that's a bit more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: But if you book before the end of this month, there's an early booking discount, so you'd only pay £185.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Great. I'll pay today, then.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: For the first class you don't need a textbook, because we provide that, but please bring a dictionary. A paper one is best, because phones aren't allowed in class.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: A dictionary, right. Is there anything else on offer for students?

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Yes. Every Saturday morning we run a free conversation session with native speakers. It's very popular with intermediate students.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: That sounds perfect. I'll definitely come along.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: Wonderful. So you're all booked. You'll get a confirmation email later today.

transcript.speaker: Daniel
transcript.text: Thanks very much for your help.

transcript.speaker: Receptionist
transcript.text: You're welcome. Goodbye.

items.title: Millbrook Riverside Park opening
items.context: A park manager talks on local radio about a new city park.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Good afternoon and welcome back to City Matters. With me in the studio is Clara Mendes, manager of the new Millbrook Riverside Park, which opens to the public this Saturday. Welcome, Clara.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Before we get to the opening, can you tell us what was on the site before?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Thank you. Well, I'd like to start with a little history, because a lot of people ask me what was on the site before.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Many people assume it used to be a factory, because of the tall brick chimney we've kept near the entrance. In fact, the chimney belonged to a small boiler house, and the whole site was a railway yard until the late nineteen-nineties.
keywords: the whole site was a railway yard

answerTags.after: the whole site was a railway yard

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: After that it was left empty for more than twenty years, and some people even used parts of it to dump rubbish.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: And it must have been an expensive project. Who paid for it?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Now, paying for the project. The city council contributed about a quarter of the cost, and several local businesses made generous donations. But the majority of the money came from a national lottery grant, and without that the park simply wouldn't exist.
keywords: the majority of the money came from a national lottery grant

answerTags.after: the majority of the money came from a national lottery grant

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Parks can be costly to look after, though.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: We also thought hard about the long-term running costs. We did discuss relying on volunteers to cut the grass, and someone even suggested bringing in sheep. In the end, rather than mowing large lawns every week, we've planted wildflower meadows, which only need cutting once a year.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Are there any rules people should know about?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: A few rules for visitors. Dogs are very welcome and can be off the lead in most areas. The one thing we ask is that people don't cycle on the riverside path, because it's quite narrow. There's a separate cycle track along the northern edge instead.
keywords: people don't cycle on the riverside path

answerTags.after: people don't cycle on the riverside path

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: And please note there's no car park at all, so we recommend coming by bus. The number 14 stops right outside.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: So what will people find when they arrive?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Let me now take you on a quick tour of the park, starting at the main entrance on Station Road.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: The first building you'll see is the Old Signal Box. We've restored it beautifully, and it's now our information centre, where you can pick up maps and find out about events.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Straight ahead is the North Meadow. It slopes gently down towards the river, which makes it a natural seating area, so we've built an outdoor theatre there, and the first play will be performed in July.
keywords: we've built an outdoor theatre there

answerTags.after: we've built an outdoor theatre there

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: That sounds lovely. What else is there?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: To the right of the meadow is the Engine Shed, the largest building on the site. Originally we planned to put a railway museum in there, but it would have been too expensive to run, so instead it's become a café with a big terrace.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: If you follow the path down to Heron Pond, you'll find a bird hide on the far side. Please keep quiet inside it, as kingfishers have been seen there most mornings.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Is there anywhere to get a view of the whole park?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Next to the pond is the Water Tower. You can't go inside the tank, of course, but we've added a staircase to a viewing platform at the top, which gives you a wonderful view across the whole city.
keywords: a viewing platform at the top

answerTags.after: a viewing platform at the top

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: Finally, at the East Gate, you'll find the bicycle hire, where you can rent a bike by the hour. Some people expected the children's play area to be there too, but we've placed that beside the main entrance, so it's easier for families arriving by bus.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: And is anything still to come?

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: We'd also hoped to open a community garden this year, but that won't be ready until next spring.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: It sounds wonderful, Clara. Thank you for coming in.

transcript.speaker: Clara
transcript.text: My pleasure. I hope to see lots of your listeners there on Saturday.

items.title: Presentation on campus food waste
items.context: Two students discuss their presentation on food waste with their tutor.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Come in, Leila, Marcus. So, how's the food waste presentation coming along?

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Pretty well, I think. We've decided to focus entirely on the main university canteen.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Why the canteen, rather than the student halls?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Well, partly because I worked there last summer, so I know how it operates. But the main reason is that the catering manager agreed to give us all their waste records, so we had easy access to the data.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: That's a real advantage. And you ran a survey as well?

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Yes. We asked students why they leave food on their plates. We expected people to say they didn't like the taste, or that they were in a hurry, but by far the most common answer was that the portions are simply too large.
keywords: the portions are simply too large

answerTags.after: the portions are simply too large

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Interesting. How many people did you survey?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Just over two hundred.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: That's a reasonable number. My concern is who they were. If most of them were first-year students, the sample isn't really representative of the whole university.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: That's true. Most of them were first-years, because we handed out the survey in the halls of residence. We'll mention that as a limitation.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Good. Now, tell me about the trayless trial.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: For two weeks, the canteen removed trays, so students could only carry one plate at a time. Some staff thought students would complain, but hardly anyone did. And it reduced food waste significantly, by about eighteen percent.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: That's a striking result. How are you planning to present your data?

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: We'd made a set of pie charts, one for each week.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Hmm. In my experience, an audience loses interest after the second or third chart.

transcript.speaker: Leila
transcript.text: Actually, we took photographs of the waste bins at the end of every day. We could show those instead. They're quite shocking.

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: Yes, use the photographs. They'll have far more impact. Keep one simple chart for the overall figures if you like.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: Did you have any problems collecting the data?

transcript.speaker: Dr Patel
transcript.text: I was going to ask you that.

transcript.speaker: Marcus
transcript.text: A couple. On several days the canteen staff forgot to separate the food waste from the packaging, so we couldn't use those figures.
keywords: the canteen staff forgot to separate the food waste

answerTags.after: the canteen staff forgot to separate the food waste

transcript.speaker: Leila

items.title: Sleep and memory
items.context: A psychology lecture on how sleep helps the brain store memories.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at one of the most active areas of research in psychology: the relationship between sleep and memory.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: For a long time, sleep was seen as a period when the brain simply switched off. We now know that's far from the truth.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One of the earliest studies took place in 1924. Two American researchers asked participants to learn lists of nonsense syllables, and then tested them some hours later.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: They found that people remembered considerably more if they had slept during that period than if they had stayed awake.
keywords: than if they had stayed awake

answerTags.after: than if they had stayed awake

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: At the time, the explanation was simply that sleep protected memories from interference. Today we believe sleep does something much more active.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: To understand this, we need to look at two brain regions. The first is the hippocampus. When we experience something new, the memory is initially held there, in what we might call a temporary buffer.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The hippocampus can't hold much information for long, though. It's a bit like a notepad rather than a filing cabinet.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: During deep, slow-wave sleep, memories are gradually transferred from the hippocampus to the cortex, where they can be stored for the long term.
keywords: from the hippocampus to the cortex

answerTags.after: from the hippocampus to the cortex

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some of the clearest evidence for this comes from animal studies. Researchers recorded the activity of individual brain cells in rats while they were running a maze.
keywords: while they were running a maze

answerTags.after: while they were running a maze

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: When the rats later fell asleep, the same pattern of activity was repeated, as if the animals were replaying the route in their sleep, only much faster.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So what about the other main stage of sleep, REM sleep, when most dreaming happens?

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: The evidence here is less clear. However, several studies suggest REM sleep is particularly important for emotional memories, helping us keep the content of an event while reducing its painful feelings.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: There's also evidence that REM sleep helps with creative thinking, and in particular with problem solving. People who slept were far more likely to discover a hidden rule in a number puzzle than those who didn't.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Now, an intriguing question is whether we can actually strengthen memories while someone is asleep.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: In one well-known experiment in Germany, participants learned the positions of pairs of cards while a smell, the scent of roses, was present in the room.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Some participants were then exposed to the same smell during slow-wave sleep. The next day, they remembered the card positions significantly better than the others.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Researchers have tried the same thing with sounds, with similar though smaller effects.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: What about daytime naps? Many people think a nap must be at least an hour to be useful. In fact, a nap of as little as twenty minutes can improve recall.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Longer naps can bring greater benefits, but they also carry the risk of waking up from deep sleep and feeling groggy for a while.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Let's turn briefly to age. As we get older, we get less deep sleep. This may partly explain why older adults often find it harder to learn new names.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: It's not the whole story, of course, but it's an important factor, and some researchers are now testing ways of boosting deep sleep in older people.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Finally, a word for students, since many of you will have exams soon. Staying up all night before an exam is a very bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: One study found that missing a night's sleep reduced the ability to form new memories by up to 40 percent.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: So my advice is simple. Rather than relying on extra hours of study late at night, go to bed at a regular time, and let your brain do some of the work for you.

transcript.speaker: Lecturer
transcript.text: Next week we'll look at dreams in more detail, so please read chapter seven before then.
